judge_assessment.explanation: The ambiguity is real, and the answer key convicts itself. worksheet.pdf problem 7 asks, on the field dy/dx = x + y drawn over a grid that runs from -4 to 4 in both variables: '(c) Draw the field at the nine lattice points nearest the origin, then say which single segment on the whole grid is steepest and why.' The slope function is x + y, so the corner (4,4) gives +8 and the corner (-4,-4) gives -8; under the ordinary geometric meaning of steepness those two segments are exactly as steep as each other. answer_key.pdf's Step 4 for that problem reads: 'The steepest segment on the grid is at the top right corner, where x and y are both as large as the grid allows and the sum x + y is therefore the largest slope drawn. The bottom left corner is equally steep downward - the field is symmetric through the origin.' The key states the tie in the sentence immediately after naming a unique winner. A student who writes (-4,-4) has given a defensible answer to a question that asked for one segment, and the key has already conceded it. The judge's other claims also hold: I re-derived every slope table (1 gives 1, 3, -3, -2; 2 gives 2, -1, -2 with the constant solution y = 2), the equilibrium and isocline solves (y = x for dy/dx = x - y, y = -x for x + y, y = 3 for (y-3)/2), the antiderivatives (x^2 for 2x with the particular solution x^2+1, and x^3/3 - x with x^3/3 - x + 1 giving 5/3 = 1.67 at x = 2), and the three manual field-sketch items, and items 1-6 and 8 are sound. One thing the judge did not reach: problems 1, 2, 4 and 7 all require the student to DRAW - segments at four lattice points, the constant-solution line, the solution curve through (1,2), and nine segments around the origin - and none of those four ids carries a manual entry, while ids 3, 5 and 8 do. The same drawn-representation demand is classified two different ways inside one verify.json, and the item that carries the hard failure (7) is on the unflagged side, so nothing in the pipeline ever asked a human to read it.

strengths_to_preserve: The isoclines are verified symbolically rather than sampled. verify.json id 5 is {"type":"solve","expr":"x - y","var":"y","expected":["x"]} and id 7 is the same shape returning ['-x'], so 'the line every horizontal segment sits on' is bound as a line, not as two lucky points on it. That is the right granularity for a slope-field sheet and it should be the house pattern.

Problem 6 makes the printed field do work the algebra cannot: the student is told to use the two columns of horizontal segments to PLACE the turning points of the solution curve through (0,1), and only then to antidifferentiate x^2 - 1 and fix the constant. The declared trap (evaluating x^3/3 - x with no constant, giving 0.67 instead of 1.67) is exactly the slip that shows a student never used the initial condition.

Problem 8's manual entry asks for a reason that the field itself supplies - why neither solution curve can cross the equilibrium line y = 3 - and pairs it with two machine-checked slopes (+1 at y = 5, -1 at y = 1) that establish the sign structure the argument needs. The open half and the checkable half are cleanly separated under one id.

root_causes.description: Problem 7(c) asks for a unique superlative on a domain where the extremum is not unique. dy/dx = x + y on a grid symmetric about the origin makes |slope| equal at (4,4) and (-4,-4), so 'which single segment ... is steepest' has two correct answers, and the key silently narrows 'steepest' to 'greatest signed slope'.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 7(c): 'say which single segment on the whole grid is steepest and why'
The printed grid spans -4 to 4 in x and y; x + y attains +8 at (4,4) and -8 at (-4,-4)
answer_key.pdf problem 7 Step 4: 'The bottom left corner is equally steep downward - the field is symmetric through the origin.'

root_causes.description: Drawn work is classified inconsistently. Ids 3, 5 and 8 carry manual entries for sketches and written justifications; ids 1, 2, 4 and 7 make the same kind of demand (draw segments, draw the constant-solution line, sketch the solution curve, draw nine segments and say which is steepest and why) and carry none, so the sheet's most error-prone item shipped with no human-review flag.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 1: 'draw a short segment of the right slope at each of those four points on the grid' - verify.json id 1 is four eval entries only
worksheet.pdf problem 4(b): 'Sketch the solution curve through (1, 2)' - verify.json id 4 is integrate plus two evals, no manual
verify.json ids 3, 5, 8 each carry {"type":"manual"} for the same class of demand

improvements.title: Problem 7 asks for the single steepest segment where two corners tie at |slope| = 8
improvements.proposed_change: Any stem that asks for 'the largest', 'the smallest', 'the steepest', 'the closest' or 'which single X' must carry a verify entry that establishes uniqueness, not just the winning value - for example a solve or a compare showing the argmax set has one element over the stated domain. When uniqueness fails, the stem must be rewritten. Here the clean repair is to ask for 'the steepest segment with positive slope' (unique at (4,4)), or to ask for 'both segments of greatest steepness' and accept the pair. SKILL.md should also carry the general rule: a superlative over a domain symmetric under the sign of the quantity has no unique answer unless the stem says signed or positive.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a stem containing 'which single segment ... is steepest' with a domain [-4,4]x[-4,4] and slope expression x + y. The new uniqueness check must exit non-zero reporting the two-element argmax {(4,4), (-4,-4)}. Rewriting the stem to 'steepest with positive slope', or changing the grid to an asymmetric one, makes it pass. Today no check exists and the packet builds green.
improvements.expected_impact: Eliminates the class of failure that rejected this case: a mathematically correct sheet whose stem promises a unique answer the mathematics does not deliver. It also protects the answer key from having to write 'X is equally steep' one line after naming a single winner.
improvements.risk: Medium. Deciding argmax uniqueness in general is hard; the check should be limited to finite declared grids and simple closed-form extrema, and fall back to demanding an explicit author assertion of uniqueness otherwise.

improvements.title: Four drawing items (1, 2, 4, 7) carry no manual entry while three others do
improvements.proposed_change: Make 'draw', 'sketch', 'plot' and 'mark' in a stem a hard trigger for a manual companion entry, so a drawn representation is never covered by the numeric entries that merely supply its inputs. On this sheet that adds manual entries under ids 1, 2, 4 and 7, matching the treatment ids 3, 5 and 8 already receive, and it puts problem 7's 'say which ... and why' in front of a human reader.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a stem containing 'draw a short segment of the right slope at each of those four points' with only eval entries under that id. verify.py must exit non-zero requiring the manual companion; adding it passes. The fixture passes today.
improvements.expected_impact: Consistent classification of drawn work across a whole packet, and a manual-review list that matches what a teacher actually has to look at on a slope-field sheet.
improvements.risk: Low. Manual counts rise on figure-heavy sheets, which the build already reports as exit 2.

case_summary: I agree with the REJECT and with the judge's reason. This is otherwise a well-made slope-field packet: eight problems moving from a slope table through reading a printed field to sketching solution curves, isoclines verified symbolically as lines rather than sampled points, a declared trap on problem 6 that catches a student who never used the initial condition, and clean, legible grids. But problem 7(c) asks for 'which single segment on the whole grid is steepest' on the field dy/dx = x + y over a grid symmetric about the origin, where (4,4) and (-4,-4) tie at |slope| = 8 - and the answer key's own Step 4 names the top-right corner and then immediately states that 'the bottom left corner is equally steep downward'. A correct student can be marked wrong by the key's own words. The judge's remaining claims all check out against the artifacts. Beyond the judge: problems 1, 2, 4 and 7 all require drawing on the printed grid and none carries a manual entry, while problems 3, 5 and 8 do - so the sheet's one defective item was also the one class of item nobody was asked to read.
